note: Event cards typed by Orbis. Dates: astronomical years (1 BC = 0); ancient dates before 45 BC follow the Roman tradition and are given as years only. Each card names its source (an ancient author and/or the Wikipedia article).

items.title: The German limes
items.text: A palisade, ditch and wall with forts and watchtowers ran about 550 km between the Rhine and the Danube. It was given up around 260.
items.source: UNESCO 'Frontiers of the Roman Empire'; Wikipedia 'Limes Germanicus'

items.title: Fossatum Africae
items.text: Ditches and walls along the edge of the Sahara controlled the movement of herders and traders; most scholars date them to the 2nd century.

items.title: Hadrian's Wall
items.text: Hadrian ordered a stone wall across northern Britain, 80 Roman miles (117 km) from the Tyne to the Solway, with a small fort every mile.

items.title: Antonine Wall
items.text: Antoninus Pius moved the frontier north to a turf wall between the Forth and the Clyde. It was abandoned after about twenty years.

items.title: Marcomannic Wars
items.text: Germanic peoples crossed the Danube and reached northern Italy. Marcus Aurelius spent most of his last years fighting on the river.

items.title: Citizens all
items.text: Caracalla made almost every free man in the empire a Roman citizen.

items.title: An emperor captured
items.text: The Persian king Shapur I captured the emperor Valerian near Edessa. In the same years breakaway states ruled the west (the Gallic Empire, 260–274) and, briefly, the east (Palmyra, 270–273).
items.source: Shapur's inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam; Wikipedia 'Crisis of the Third Century'

items.title: Dacia given up
items.text: Aurelian withdrew from Dacia north of the Danube, the first province Rome abandoned.

items.title: Four emperors
items.text: Diocletian shared power with three co-emperors, each with his own capital: Nicomedia, Sirmium, Mediolanum and Augusta Treverorum.

items.title: Constantinople
items.text: Constantine refounded Byzantium as his new capital and named it after himself, dedicating it on 11 May 330.

items.title: Adrianople
items.text: Goths who had crossed the Danube destroyed an eastern Roman army and killed the emperor Valens.

items.title: Two empires
items.text: Theodosius I died in January 395. His sons split the empire: Arcadius ruled the east from Constantinople, Honorius the west from Mediolanum and later Ravenna.
